unit.unitOverview: Collaboration is working with other people towards a shared goal, sharing the work fairly and helping each other, so that together you produce something better than any of you could alone. It is not just being in the same room. Real collaboration means agreeing a goal, dividing roles fairly, contributing useful ideas backed by evidence, listening and building on each other, resolving disagreement, and reviewing honestly how you worked.

explainers.title: Welcome back to Global Perspectives
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome to Unit 5 of Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. By now you know this subject is not about memorising facts. It teaches you a set of thinking and working skills that you can carry into any subject, any job, and any part of your life.

There are six skills in Global Perspectives, and you keep growing all of them, year after year:

This unit is about the fifth skill: Collaboration. Most of your Global Perspectives work so far has been something you could do largely on your own: researching, analysing, evaluating and reflecting. Collaboration is different. You cannot collaborate by yourself. It is the skill of getting good things done with other people — agreeing a shared goal, sharing the work fairly, listening closely, handling disagreement well, and finishing something together that no single person could have built alone.

In Stage 8 you go further than before. It is not enough simply to be in a team and be pleasant. This year you will divide roles by thinking carefully about each person's strengths and the time you have; you will make sure the ideas your team puts forward are backed by reasoning and evidence, not just opinion; you will resolve real disagreements and solve problems as they come up; you will give and receive specific feedback; and you will step back and judge honestly how well your team worked, including your own part in it. These are the moves of a genuinely effective team.

Why does this matter beyond school? Almost everything important in the adult world is built by teams. A road is made safer when a community, its drivers and the local authority agree on a plan and act on it. People who collaborate well get chosen for the best work, and they get more done. That is why we practise it here, on purpose, until it becomes natural.
bullets: Research — finding things out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — taking a topic apart to see its causes, effects and connections.
Evaluation — judging how strong an argument or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking honestly about how you learn and how your views change.
Collaboration — working well with other people towards a shared goal.
Communication — sharing your ideas so clearly that others truly understand.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit: a special split
explainers.body:
You are learning the Ehel Academy way, which is self-paced. Three kinds of support work together for you:

Collaboration needs one careful change to this model, and it is the most important idea in the whole unit. You cannot truly collaborate with a book, and you cannot truly collaborate alone. Real collaboration needs real people. So in this unit your learning splits neatly into two halves:

So all through this unit you will see the same rhythm: plan it with your AI tutor now, then carry it out with your group in your next teacher session. Think of your AI tutor as the training ground and your teacher session as the real match. An athlete who trains hard alone performs far better on the day. In the same way, a learner who rehearses teamwork with their tutor becomes a much stronger teammate when the real people are in the room.

Here is what that looks like in practice. Before a teacher session, you might tell your AI tutor: I think my group will disagree about whether our presentation should focus on drivers or on the school. You then ask it to help you prepare a calm way to suggest a compromise, and you practise the exact words, so that when the disagreement really happens you are ready and steady.
bullets: You, learning at your own pace. You read, think and prepare in your own time.
Your AI tutor, available every hour of the day. It is your study partner and, in this unit, your planning and rehearsal partner.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In live sessions you meet the other learners and do the real teamwork face to face.

Plan and rehearse with your AI tutor. On your own time, you use your tutor to get ready. You plan the roles, sharpen your ideas into claims backed by evidence, practise active listening, rehearse how you will disagree politely and solve a problem, and get feedback before anyone else hears it. Your tutor can even pretend to be a difficult teammate so you can practise safely.

Do the real collaboration with people. The actual teamwork happens in your twice-weekly teacher sessions, where you work face to face with your group, and at home, where you work with your family and community.

explainers.title: Meet the group we will follow this unit
explainers.body:
Because this unit is about teamwork, we will follow a whole group of Year 8 learners at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. They are an ordinary team, with ordinary strengths and ordinary disagreements. There is no single leader among them, and that is deliberate: in a strong team, leadership is shared, and different people step forward for different jobs.

Notice that no one in this group is good at everything, and that is completely normal. A strong team is not five people who are all the same. It is different people whose strengths fit together, so the team as a whole can do what no single member could. As you meet each skill, watch how this group uses each person's strength, and how they make sure Dina, their quietest member, is properly heard.

You will also watch them disagree, get stuck, and get a few things wrong along the way, because that is what real teams do. What makes them effective is not that they never struggle. It is that they keep working together honestly and kindly until they get there, and your own team will be just the same.
bullets: Talia is organised. She likes making a plan, keeping track of who is doing what, and watching the deadline so the team does not run out of time.
Nadir is full of ideas. He is creative and enjoys suggesting new ways to do things, though he is still learning that not every idea will fit the goal.
Grace is a warm listener. She notices when someone has gone quiet and gently brings them back into the conversation, which keeps the whole team calm.
Malik is confident speaking to an audience. He is comfortable presenting the team's work clearly, and he is good at encouraging the others when energy dips.
Dina is careful and thoughtful. She likes to check that every claim the team makes is backed by real evidence, and she is quieter, so her ideas can be missed unless the team makes space for her.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: a shared group project
explainers.body:
This unit builds towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge. In earlier units your Challenge was mostly yours alone. In this unit it becomes a shared outcome: something your whole group plans, builds and finishes together, such as a presentation, a poster or a short video that raises awareness about a real problem.

Here are some issues that are global and also very real in the Horn of Africa. Any of these could become your group's shared Challenge:

The group we follow chose road safety. They noticed that the street outside Ehel Academy in Hargeisa becomes dangerous at the start and end of the school day: cars and bajaaj taxis pass quickly, there is no safe place to cross, and younger children weave between the traffic. Their shared outcome will be a visual presentation for the school community, urging drivers to slow down at school times and calling for a safe crossing. You will watch them build it, skill by skill.

Their aim gives the project its direction. An aim is the purpose of a shared outcome; it answers the question, what are we hoping to achieve? The group's aim is to persuade drivers and the school to make the crossing safer. Everything they build has to serve that aim, which is why they choose a persuasive presentation rather than, say, a simple list of facts.

Your topic will probably be different, and that is good. Another group of learners at Ehel Academy in Mogadishu chose healthy school meals, and a third group chose saving water in the dry season. Whatever your group picks, you will use exactly the same collaboration skills to build it together. You will agree your own topic and aim as a team in a teacher session, so for now just keep a note of any local problem that makes you curious or a little annoyed, because those feelings often point to a strong shared Challenge.
bullets: Road safety on busy streets, especially near schools
Clean, safe water for every family
Cutting waste and keeping our streets and coast clean
Keeping children, especially girls, in school
Saving energy, or using solar power
Protecting wildlife, such as sea turtles on the Berbera coast
Healthy food and better school meals

explainers.title: What is collaboration, really?
explainers.body:
Many people think teamwork just means being in the same room while everyone does their own thing. Real collaboration is far more than that. Collaboration is a group of people agreeing on a shared goal, sharing the work fairly, and helping each other so that together they produce something better than any of them could alone.

Good collaboration usually moves through a cycle:

You will learn every step in this unit. Notice that collaboration is not simply about being nice. It is a set of skills you can practise and improve, exactly like research. Collaboration is a skill, not a fixed personality, which means anyone can get better at it. And like research, you already do it in everyday life without calling it a skill.

Nobody is a perfect teammate, and you will sometimes catch yourself in an unhelpful habit. That is fine; noticing it is the first step to changing it.
bullets: Agree on a clear shared goal, and the aim behind it, that everyone understands.
Work out each person's strengths and agree who does what, fairly.
Contribute useful ideas, backed by reasoning and evidence, towards the goal.
Listen actively and build on each other's ideas.
Resolve any disagreement respectfully, and solve problems together.
Produce the shared outcome, then improve it using feedback.
Review honestly how well the team worked, and set targets to do better next time.
Effective teammates share useful ideas, listen to others, follow through on their tasks, encourage quieter members, back up their claims with reasons and evidence, and stay calm when they disagree.
Unhelpful habits include complaining without helping, disappearing when there is work to do, always needing to be in charge, refusing to compromise, and arguing just to win.

explainers.title: A Stage 8 habit: claims, reasoning and evidence
explainers.body:
Before you meet the team skills, learn one habit that runs through the whole of Stage 8 and makes your teamwork far stronger. Whenever your team says something is true, you are making a claim. A claim on its own is weak, because anyone can claim anything. To be trusted, a claim needs two supports:

In a team, this habit stops your shared outcome from being just a set of opinions. When one member says 'our street is dangerous', a good team asks, what is your reasoning, and what is your evidence? The claim only belongs in the presentation once it has both.
bullets: Reasoning answers the question, why do I think this? It is the thinking that links your claim to your evidence.
Evidence answers the question, how do I know this? It is the facts, the observations or the interviews that show the claim is true.

explainers.title: Keep a teamwork journal
explainers.body:
Start a simple habit that strong teams use: keep a teamwork journal. This can be a notebook or a document where you record how your group works together as you go. Each time your team meets, write the date and jot down what your role was, what you contributed, any disagreement and how you solved it, and one thing you want to do better next time.

A teamwork journal matters for three reasons. It helps you see your own part honestly, which you will need for Reflection. It reminds the whole group what you agreed, so nothing gets forgotten between sessions. And it makes the final team review far easier, because the story of your teamwork is already written down. Keep your journal beside you as you work through this unit.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Knowing your strengths and agreeing roles fairly
explainers.body:
Every strong team starts by working out who is good at what, then dividing the tasks fairly. This is the heart of Cambridge objective 5.1: the team assigns roles and divides tasks fairly, considering the skills of the team members and the time available, and works together to achieve a shared outcome.

Fair does not mean everyone does exactly the same thing. It means the work is shared so that no one is overloaded and no one is left with nothing to do, so that people can use their strengths while still stretching a little, and so that every job fits the time you actually have before the deadline. To agree roles well, a team asks three questions:
bullets: What are our strengths? Who is good at organising, listening, being creative, presenting, checking evidence, meeting deadlines, or encouraging others?
What tasks does our shared outcome need? List every job that must be done for the presentation to be finished.
How much time do we have? Match the size of each job to the time available, so nothing important is left until it is too late.

explainers.title: Skill 2: Contributing useful ideas backed by reasoning and evidence
explainers.body:
A team is only as good as the ideas its members bring. Cambridge objective 5.2 asks each team member to introduce useful ideas that help achieve the shared outcome. The key word is useful. A useful idea is not just any idea; it is one that is relevant to your goal and that you can support with reasoning and evidence.

You do not have to be the loudest person to contribute well. A quiet member who offers one sharp, relevant, well-supported idea contributes more than someone who talks constantly but says little. Before you share an idea, check it twice: does it fit our goal, and can I back it up?

explainers.title: Skill 3: Active listening and encouraging everyone to take part
explainers.body:
Collaboration is at least as much about listening as it is about talking. Active listening means showing the speaker that you have really heard them, not just waiting for your turn to speak. It is one of the most powerful team skills you can build, and it is what makes a group feel safe enough for everyone to share.

Active listening has a few simple moves:

That last move, building on an idea, is what turns a group of individuals into a real team. When you say 'Yes, and ...', you take someone's idea and add to it, so the idea grows and the person feels valued. Active listening is also how you meet the part of objective 5.2 about encouraging other team members to participate, which matters most for your quietest members, who often hold the ideas nobody else has thought of.
bullets: Look at the speaker and do not interrupt while they are talking.
Show you heard them by briefly repeating their idea back: 'So you are saying we should ...'.
Ask a question to understand more, rather than jumping straight to your own point.
Build on the idea using words like 'Yes, and ...' instead of 'No, but ...'.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Resolving disagreement and solving problems together
explainers.body:
Every real team disagrees sometimes, and that is not a bad sign. Disagreement, handled well, can make an idea stronger. The part of objective 5.2 about working positively to resolve conflict and solve issues is not about never arguing; it is about arguing over the idea, kindly, and then reaching an agreement the whole team can accept.

Three habits keep a disagreement healthy:

It helps to have sentence starters ready, so that in the heat of the moment you can disagree without sounding rude. Phrases such as 'I see your point, and I wonder if ...' or 'What if we combined both ideas by ...' let you push back on an idea gently. You will find a full list in your Skills Toolkit.
bullets: Separate the idea from the person. You can disagree with an idea while still respecting the person who offered it.
Look for the compromise. Very often two different ideas can be combined into a better third idea that uses the best of both.
Try to see the other point of view, even one you do not share at first. Understanding why someone thinks something is the fastest route to agreement.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Building a shared outcome that fits its aim and audience
explainers.body:
Once the ideas are agreed, your team turns them into the shared outcome itself. Two Stage 8 questions keep the outcome strong: does it fit its aim, and does it suit its audience? A shared outcome should be the right tool for the job. A persuasive presentation suits an aim of changing people's minds, just as a clear poster suits an aim of reminding people of one message. If the form does not match the aim, even good content will miss.

A strong shared outcome usually has these features, and a good team checks for each one together:

There is one more part many teams forget: how you present it. How you present matters almost as much as what you say. Speak clearly and not too fast, make eye contact with the audience, stand so people can see the visuals, and make sure every member of the team has a real part to play. A presentation where one confident person does everything is weaker, and less fair, than one the whole team delivers together.
bullets: A clear structure with a beginning, a middle and an end, so the audience can follow it.
A mix of visuals, such as text, images and a simple chart, sized so the audience can read them.
Content that answers the question and stays relevant to the aim.
Claims supported by reasoning and evidence, not just opinions.
A contribution from every member, so it is genuinely shared work.

explainers.title: Skill 6: Giving and receiving specific feedback
explainers.body:
Once your team has a draft, feedback makes it better, and in Stage 8 the feedback becomes more specific. Feedback is honest, kind, specific advice about a piece of work, meant to help improve it. Learning to give feedback well, and to receive it without getting upset, is one of the most grown-up team skills you can develop.

A simple, fair way to give feedback is two stars and a wish: name two things that work well (the stars), then one thing that could be better (the wish). Three rules keep your feedback helpful:

In Stage 8 you often give feedback by evaluating another team's presentation against clear criteria: were the visuals suitable, was the structure clear, were the claims supported with evidence, did the presenters make eye contact and speak clearly, and was every member involved? Judging work against criteria like these makes your feedback fair and specific rather than just a feeling.

Receiving feedback well is its own skill. When someone gives you feedback, listen without interrupting, thank them, resist the urge to defend your work, and then choose one thing to act on. Remember that feedback is about the work, not about you as a person.
bullets: Focus on the work, not the person. Say 'the third slide has a lot of text', not 'you wrote too much'.
Be kind but honest. Kindness without honesty does not help the team improve; honesty without kindness just hurts.
Be specific and useful. Instead of 'make it better', say 'the claim on slide two needs evidence; could you add the traffic count?'.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Reviewing and improving how the team works
explainers.body:
When the shared outcome is finished, an effective team does one more thing: it looks back honestly at how it worked together. This is where Collaboration meets Reflection. In Stage 8 you review two things carefully: how effective the team was as a whole, and how well each member, including you, played their own role.

An honest team review asks questions like these:

The most important word here is honest. A review that says 'everything was perfect' teaches you nothing. A review that admits 'we let one person do most of the presenting' is far more useful, because it shows the team exactly what to do better next time. Reviewing your own role honestly, and reflecting fairly on the roles of others, is a strength, not a weakness.
bullets: Did we finish our shared outcome on time?
Did everyone contribute and feel listened to?
Did we support our claims with reasoning and evidence?
How well did we resolve disagreements and solve problems?
Did we use the feedback we received to improve our work?
What did we do best, and what should we improve next time?

explainers.title: How collaboration links to the other five skills
explainers.body:
Collaboration does not stand alone. It pulls together every other Global Perspectives skill and makes each one stronger.

You can see all six skills at work in our group at once. They researched the traffic on their street, analysed which change would help most, evaluated the feedback another team gave them, reflected on how well they worked, and will soon communicate their presentation to the whole school. Collaboration was the thread that tied every other skill together.
bullets: Research feeds your team, because a member who brings well-researched evidence is far more useful than one who guesses.
Analysis helps you break the shared task into parts and roles, so the work can be divided fairly.
Evaluation lets your team judge which idea is strongest, weigh the feedback you receive, and check that claims have real evidence.
Reflection grows every time your team reviews honestly how it worked together.
Communication is how your team shares its outcome clearly, so all your teamwork actually reaches an audience.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the collaboration cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every collaboration skill in this unit. Here is how they fit into one smooth cycle you can use for any team task:
bullets: Agree a clear shared goal and aim that everyone understands.
Work out your strengths and divide the roles fairly, by strength and time (objective 5.1).
Contribute useful, relevant ideas backed by reasoning and evidence (objective 5.2).
Listen actively, build on each other's ideas, and encourage everyone to take part.
Resolve disagreement respectfully and solve problems together (objective 5.2).
Produce a shared outcome that fits its aim and audience, then improve it using feedback.
Review honestly how well the team worked, and set targets for next time.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Communication. Once your team can work together well, communication teaches you to share your shared outcome clearly and convincingly, so that all your teamwork actually changes how an audience thinks and acts. Strong collaboration now will make strong communication much easier later. Well done for learning to build things with other people, which is one of the most valuable skills you will ever have.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to hold on to
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is the vehicle and the skill is the destination.
In this unit your group will work on a real issue, such as road safety or clean water in your community.
But the point is not the issue. The point is to become a person who can work well in any team, on anything, for the rest of your life.

bigIdeas.title: Being fair to different perspectives, and avoiding bias
lines: Global Perspectives is about working respectfully with people who see the world differently from you. Bias is judging from only one point of view and refusing to consider others.

A biased campaign would only interview people who already agree with the team. To stay fair, the group made sure to hear a range of neighbours, including Muslim and Christian families, market sellers, parents and drivers.
When they planned a short awareness event, they chose a time that respected both Friday prayers and Sunday worship, so families of different faiths could all take part.
Gathering evidence from many perspectives, and reaching agreement across different beliefs without pushing one side, is at the very heart of collaboration.

bigIdeas.title: Two stars and a wish
lines: Star 1: One thing the work does well.
Star 2: A second thing the work does well.
Wish: One specific thing that would make it better, such as: the claim on slide two needs evidence; could you add the traffic count?
Sentence starters you can use when you give feedback, so it stays kind and specific:

bigIdeas.title: Remember the split all the way through
lines: Your AI tutor is your training ground: plan roles, sharpen ideas into claims with evidence, rehearse listening, and try out feedback safely with it first.
Your teacher session is the real match: that is where the actual teamwork with your group happens.
Plan it with your tutor now, then carry it out with your group next.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 5 of Stage 8 Global Perspectives, and the skill is Collaboration.
Ask it: Why is being able to work well with other people such a valuable skill in the adult world?
Then say: In this unit, please be my planning and rehearsal partner. I will get ready with you, then do the real teamwork with my group in my teacher sessions.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you now think collaboration means.
Ask the tutor: Is my definition missing anything important?
Then tell it one habit of an effective teammate you are already good at, and one you would like to get better at this unit.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your shared Challenge idea and the strengths you think you bring to a team.
Ask it to help you list every job a presentation on your topic would need, and roughly how long each one might take.
Rehearse a fair split that matches strengths to jobs. Afterwards, agree the real roles together with your group in your next teacher session.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your group's shared goal, then brainstorm five possible ideas with it.
Ask the tutor: Which of my ideas are most relevant to the goal, and which could I actually back up with reasoning and evidence?
Rehearse offering your best idea in one clear sentence, with the reason and evidence ready. Then share it with your real group in your teacher session.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to role-play a teammate sharing an idea, while you practise active listening.
Practise repeating the idea back, asking one question, and then building on it with the words Yes, and.
Ask the tutor for feedback on your listening. Then use these same moves, especially inviting your quietest member in by name, with your real group in your teacher session.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a disagreement your group might have, then ask it to argue the opposite side to you.
Practise staying calm, using a polite sentence starter, and offering a compromise that combines both ideas.
When a real disagreement or problem comes up in your teacher session, use what you rehearsed to help your group reach agreement.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your aim and your audience, then ask: does a presentation, a poster or a video best suit this aim?
Ask it to check your plan against the features of a strong outcome: structure, visuals, relevance, evidence, and a part for everyone.
Rehearse your own speaking part aloud, then ask the tutor for feedback on your clarity and pace. Deliver it with your group in your teacher session.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe your draft outcome to your AI tutor and ask it to give you two stars and a wish, judged against clear criteria.
Practise receiving the wish calmly: thank it, and name one specific change you could make.
Rehearse giving kind, specific feedback on an imagined presentation too. Then swap real feedback with another group in your teacher session.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Talk through an honest self-review with your AI tutor: what did you contribute, and what will you do better next time?
Ask it to help you turn one honest thought into a fair, specific target, and to help you reflect kindly on a teammate's role too.
Then complete the team review together with your group in your teacher session, and compare what each of you noticed.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your top three characteristics and your reasons.
Ask it: Which of these ten habits build a team up, and which pull it down?
Then tell the tutor which helpful habit you already show, and which one you would like to grow this unit.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor two or three local problems you care about, from the list in the Lesson file or your own.
Ask it: Which of these would make a good shared group project, and what aim could we set, meaning what would we hope to achieve?
Rehearse how you will suggest your favourite to your group kindly, and how you will listen to theirs.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which team skills you are strong at: organising, listening, being creative, presenting, checking evidence, meeting deadlines, or encouraging others.
Ask it to help you list every job your shared outcome will need, and roughly how long each one will take.
Rehearse suggesting a fair split, and practise offering to take a job that fits your strength.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Remind your AI tutor of your shared goal, then brainstorm at least five ideas for your outcome with it.
Take your strongest idea and turn it into a claim. Ask the tutor to help you add the reasoning (why you think it) and the evidence (how you know it).
Rehearse explaining that claim, reason and evidence in two or three clear sentences.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to pretend to be a teammate and share an idea about your topic.
Practise the moves: do not interrupt, repeat the idea back, ask a question, then build on it with the words Yes, and.
Ask the tutor for feedback: did you really listen, or were you just waiting to talk?

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe a disagreement your group might have, then ask your AI tutor to argue the opposite side to you.
Practise a polite sentence starter, such as: I see your point, and I wonder if we could combine both ideas.
Keep going until you and the tutor reach a compromise that uses the best of both ideas.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your topic and draft five interview questions about it.
Ask it to check that your questions are clear and fair, and not leading toward one answer.
Ask the tutor who you should interview so your evidence reflects the whole community, not just one view.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what form your outcome will take and which part is your job.
Ask it to check your plan against the features of a strong outcome, and whether the form suits your aim.
Rehearse your own speaking part aloud, and ask the tutor for feedback on your clarity, pace and eye contact.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe your draft outcome to your AI tutor and ask it to evaluate it against clear criteria, then give two stars and a wish.
Practise receiving the wish calmly: thank it, and name one specific change you will make.
Then rehearse giving kind, specific feedback on an imagined presentation, focusing on the work and not the person.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Give your AI tutor an honest self-review of your own role: what did you contribute, and what could you do better?
Ask it to help you turn one honest thought into a fair, specific target, and to reflect kindly on a teammate's role too.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three Challenge sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Based on our teamwork, what is one thing our group could do even better next time?
Ask the tutor to help you plan how you will raise that idea with your group kindly.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your rewritten feedback, your supported claims, and your respectful sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your feedback is now specific and about the work, and whether your claims now have reasoning and evidence.
Ask the tutor to show you one more way to reword any line you found hard.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to tell you which answer showed the strongest teamwork thinking, and why.
Ask the tutor to give you one more team scenario like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your reflection answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how you grew as a teammate from the start of the unit to now.
Ask the tutor to suggest one collaboration habit to focus on in the next unit, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: A human touch
lines: Ask a family member which local problem they most wish the community would fix together.
Bring their answer, and your own ideas, to your next teacher session.
Your group can then compare everyone's ideas and agree on one shared Challenge, and its aim, together.

speakingPrompts.title: A real-world step
lines: With a trusted adult's help, ask your agreed questions to a few family members or neighbours.
Bring what you find back to your next teacher session so the team can use it as evidence in the shared outcome.

teacherSessions.title: Collaboration happens in everyday life too
lines: Imagine your family is preparing a big meal to welcome guests for a celebration.
You agree the shared goal: a good meal, ready on time. You share the work by strength: one person shops, one cooks, one cleans, one welcomes the guests.
You listen to each other, you sort out the moment when two people both need the one pot, and you finish together.
That is real collaboration, and you already do it. This unit just helps you do it on purpose, with more skill, on a project that matters to your community.
Part of collaboration is knowing what an effective teammate looks like. Some habits build a team up, and some pull it down.

teacherSessions.title: Dina turns a claim into a strong point
lines: Nadir says the street outside school is dangerous. That is a claim, and on its own it is only an opinion.
Dina helps him add reasoning: it is dangerous because vehicles pass quickly at exactly the times children are crossing.
Then she helps him add evidence: in ten minutes after school, the team counted twenty-two vehicles and only three slowed down, and a shopkeeper described two near-misses last month.
Now the point is strong. Claim, reasoning and evidence together are far more convincing than a claim alone, and this is what Stage 8 asks of your team.
You will use this claim-reasoning-evidence habit again and again in this unit: when you contribute ideas, when you build your presentation, and when you give feedback on someone else's work.

teacherSessions.title: The group divides the road-safety roles fairly
lines: The team lists the jobs their presentation will need: a plan and a timeline, some real interviews and an observation count, a check that every claim has evidence, the slides and visuals, and a confident presenter.
Talia, who is organised, agrees to coordinate the plan and the deadlines. Nadir, who is creative, will design the slides and visuals. Malik, who is confident, will lead the presenting.

Grace, a warm listener, will interview neighbours and the bajaaj drivers about the street. Dina, careful with detail, will run the ten-minute traffic count and check that each claim on the slides has reasoning and evidence.
Every member has a fair share that fits their strength and the time available, and nobody is left out. That is objective 5.1 in action.
Notice two things the group did. They matched each role to a real strength, and they made sure Dina, their quietest member, had a genuinely important job rather than a leftover one.

teacherSessions.title: Nadir contributes ideas, and the team weighs them
lines: Nadir, who loves ideas, suggests three things for the road-safety presentation: a large photo of the crossing at pick-up time, a simple chart of the traffic count, and a long list of every road rule in the country.
The team keeps the photo, because it shows the local problem clearly and fits the aim of persuading people.

They keep the chart, because it turns Dina's traffic count into evidence anyone can see at a glance. They drop the long list of rules, because it is not relevant to their street and would bury the message.
Nadir is not upset that one idea was dropped. Offering three ideas so the team can choose the best, and judging each against the goal, is exactly how a good member contributes.

See how the team judged each idea against the goal and the evidence, not against the person who said it? Ideas are not good or bad because of who offered them. They are useful or not useful depending on whether they help the shared outcome and can be supported.

teacherSessions.title: Grace listens Dina into the conversation
lines: The team is stuck for the strongest single message for the presentation. Dina says quietly, almost to herself, maybe we should lead with the traffic count.
Grace notices. Instead of talking over her, she looks at Dina and repeats it back: so you are saying we open with the number of vehicles that did not slow down.
Then she builds on it: yes, and we could put that number in huge letters on the first slide, so the audience feels the problem straight away.

Dina, feeling heard, adds more: and we can show the shopkeeper's words underneath as evidence. Her quiet idea became the opening of the whole presentation, because Grace listened and made space for her.

teacherSessions.title: Talia and Malik disagree, then solve the problem
lines: Talia wants the presentation to focus on the drivers, because they are the ones speeding. Malik wants it to focus on the school, because the school could pay for a crossing.

Instead of arguing to win, Malik says: I see why the drivers matter, and I still think the school can actually change things. Talia replies: what if we speak to both, and end by asking the drivers to slow down and the school to add a crossing?
They combine both ideas into a stronger presentation with two clear requests. The problem of who to aim at is solved, and neither person lost.
They separated the idea from the person, looked for a compromise, and reached agreement. That is objective 5.2 at its best.

teacherSessions.title: The group shapes and shares its presentation
lines: The team checks their draft against the aim: does this persuade drivers and the school to make the crossing safer? They cut a slide about car engines that was interesting but did not serve the aim.
They give it a clear shape: the problem first, shown by Dina's traffic count; then the local voices from Grace's interviews; then their two clear requests.

They share the presenting instead of leaving it all to Malik. Malik opens and closes, Dina explains the evidence, Nadir talks through the visuals, Talia keeps them to time, and Grace shares what the neighbours said.
Because every member has a speaking part and the form fits the aim, the presentation is stronger and it is truly the whole team's work.

teacherSessions.title: The group swaps feedback with another team
lines: Another team, led by Amara and Kian, evaluates the draft presentation against the criteria. Their two stars: the opening traffic count is powerful, and every member had a clear speaking part.
Their wish: one slide made a strong claim about drivers with no evidence behind it, which weakened an otherwise convincing case.
Malik feels a flash of wanting to argue, but instead the group thanks the other team and talks it over. Dina adds the shopkeeper's words as evidence for that claim.
The final presentation is much stronger, all because the team received specific feedback and acted on it instead of taking it personally.

teacherSessions.title: The group reviews its teamwork
lines: The team fills in a review grid together. They finished on time, everyone had a speaking part, and every major claim ended up supported with evidence. Those are real strengths.
But Talia honestly notes that at the start, the team almost forgot to give Dina space, and two members kept talking over each other.
So the team agrees on one thing to improve next time: let one person speak at a time, and check early that the quietest member has been heard.

Each member also reviews their own role and the others' roles fairly. Nadir admits he pushed his ideas a little too hard; the team notes that Dina's careful checking is what made their evidence trustworthy.

teacherSessions.title: The group's whole journey, from problem to campaign
lines: Skill 1: They matched their strengths to roles and made sure even Dina had a real, important job.
Skill 2: Each member brought useful ideas, and the team kept the ones that fit the goal and had evidence.
Skill 3: Grace listened Dina into the conversation, and her idea became the opening of the presentation.
Skill 4: Talia and Malik disagreed about the audience, then combined both ideas into two clear requests.
Skills 5 and 6: They built a presentation that fit their aim, shared the presenting, and made it stronger with another team's feedback.
Skill 7: They reviewed their teamwork honestly and agreed one clear thing to improve next time.

By following this cycle, an ordinary group of learners turned a worry about a dangerous street into a real campaign they built together. In the Activities file, you will run the same cycle with your own group, planning each step with your AI tutor and carrying it out with real people.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Share your rankings with your team and compare them.
As a team, agree on the three characteristics you most want everyone to show.
Notice how your team reached agreement when your rankings were different.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Each member shares one topic idea and one reason they care about it.
As a team, agree on one shared Challenge, then write one sentence stating your aim.
Notice how you reached agreement, and whether the person whose topic was not chosen still feels part of the team.

Agreeing a topic and an aim is your team's first taste of compromise. If two members wanted different topics, notice how you decided fairly. That feeling of still belonging matters more than the topic itself, because the person whose idea was not chosen still has to help build the outcome.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: As a team, fill in the roles-and-responsibilities table from your Skills Toolkit.
For each member, write their strength, their role, their main task, and a deadline.
Check together: is the work shared fairly, does it fit the time, and does everyone, including your quietest member, have a real job?
Write the finished roles into your teamwork journal, so no one forgets what they agreed to do.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Each member offers their best idea as a claim, with a reason and any evidence. Nobody judges an idea by who said it.
As a team, decide which claims fit the goal and are well supported enough to belong in your outcome.
In your journal, note one claim you contributed and one from someone else that you helped strengthen with evidence.

Notice who found it easy to let an idea go, and who found it hard. Both feelings are completely normal. Letting go of your own idea for the good of the team is a real teamwork skill, and it gets easier every time you do it.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Run a short team discussion where each person must repeat the previous idea before adding their own.
Make a point of inviting your quietest member to speak by name, and build on what they say.
Afterwards, ask each other: did everyone feel listened to?

If someone felt talked over, that is useful to know rather than something to feel bad about. Agree one small change together, such as letting each person finish before the next person speaks, and try it in your next session.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: When a real disagreement comes up, use the sentence starters instead of arguing to win.
Look for a compromise that combines both ideas rather than choosing one winner.
In your journal, record what the disagreement was and how your team solved it.

The goal of a disagreement is never to win, but to reach a decision the whole team can live with. A compromise that everyone accepts is far stronger than a victory that leaves one person feeling ignored.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: As a team, share everyone's questions and agree on the best five to use.
Decide who will ask whom, and make sure your list includes a range of people so your evidence is not one-sided.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Bring each person's part together into one draft outcome.
Check as a team: does every claim have evidence, does the form fit the aim, and has everyone contributed?
Agree who will say which part when you present, so the presenting is shared, not left to one person.

Before you call the draft finished, check it against a simple list together: a clear structure; a mix of words and images; text large enough to read; content that answers your question with evidence; and a speaking part for everyone. Fix anything missing as a team.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Swap your draft with another group and evaluate each other against the presentation criteria in your Skills Toolkit.
Give each other two stars and a wish, and check that your wish is specific and about the work.
Receive their feedback without arguing; thank them, and as a team make one clear improvement based on it.

teacherSessions.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Complete the team-review grid from your Skills Toolkit together.
Agree on one thing your team did best and one thing to improve next time.
Reflect on each member's role fairly. Being honest here is a strength, not a weakness.

Write your team's review into your teamwork journal. A team that reviews honestly, session after session, gets visibly better each time; a team that skips this step tends to keep repeating the same mistakes without noticing.

toolkit.title: The collaboration cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your task, good teamwork follows the same seven steps. Come back to this list whenever your team feels stuck.
items: Agree the goal and aim: make sure everyone understands the shared outcome and its purpose.
Share the roles: divide tasks fairly by strengths and time (objective 5.1).
Contribute ideas: offer useful, relevant ideas backed by reasoning and evidence (objective 5.2).
Listen and build: hear each other out, build on ideas with 'Yes, and ...', and encourage everyone.
Resolve and solve: argue about the idea, kindly, and solve problems together (objective 5.2).
Produce and improve: build an outcome that fits its aim, then improve it using feedback.
Review: look back honestly at how the team, and you, worked, and set a target.

toolkit.title: The Collaboration skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Collaboration is working with other people towards a shared goal, sharing the work fairly and helping each other, so that together you produce something better than any of you could alone. It is not just being in the same room. Real collaboration means agreeing a goal, dividing roles fairly, contributing useful ideas backed by evidence, listening and building on each other, resolving disagreement, and reviewing honestly how you worked.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, value every member, because a team is stronger when everyone, even the quietest person, contributes. Second, focus on the idea, not the person, whether you are choosing ideas, disagreeing, or giving feedback. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 8 Collaboration objectives
toolkit.intro: Global Perspectives sets out exactly what strong collaboration looks like at this stage. There are two Collaboration objectives, and every lesson in this unit works on them both. Here they are, restated simply. Your teacher may refer to these codes.

rows: The team assign roles and divide tasks fairly, considering the skills of team members and time available, and work together to achieve a shared outcome.
Work out who is good at what, share the jobs fairly by strength and time, and pull together to make one shared outcome.
The team member introduces useful ideas to help achieve a shared outcome and works positively to resolve conflict, solve issues and encourage other team members to participate, when required.
Bring useful, well-supported ideas, sort out disagreements kindly, help solve problems, and encourage others to join in.

toolkit.title: Claims, reasoning and evidence
toolkit.intro:
In Stage 8, the ideas and points your team puts into a shared outcome should be supported, not just stated. Whenever you say something is true, you are making a claim. Back every claim with two things.

Use this whenever you contribute an idea, build your outcome, or give feedback. A claim with reasoning and evidence is one of the clearest signs of a Stage 8 team.

rows: Claim
A statement that something is true.
The street outside our school is dangerous at home time.
Reasoning
Why you think the claim is true; it answers 'Why do I think this?'.
Because vehicles pass quickly at exactly the time children are crossing.
Evidence
How you know the claim is true; it answers 'How do I know this?'.
In ten minutes we counted 22 vehicles and only 3 slowed; a shopkeeper described two near-misses.

toolkit.title: Effective and unhelpful team habits
toolkit.intro: Every team is made of people, and people have habits. These build a team up or pull it down. Aim for the left column, and gently notice when you slip into the right.

rows: Shares useful, supported ideas
Complains without helping
Listens to others
Talks over people
Follows through on tasks
Disappears when there is work
Encourages quieter members
Always needs to be in charge
Stays calm in disagreement
Argues just to win
Is creative and flexible
Refuses to compromise

toolkit.title: Roles you might take in a team
toolkit.intro:
There is no single right set of roles, but most teams need these jobs covered. One person can hold more than one role, and a fair team makes sure every member, including the quietest, holds a real one.

When you agree roles, match each one to a real strength, but do not be afraid to stretch: a quieter member might try presenting a small part, with the team's support.
items: Coordinator — keeps the plan, tracks who is doing what, and watches the deadline.
Ideas person — suggests new ways to do things and offers options to choose from.
Researcher — gathers the facts, the local views and the evidence the outcome will need.
Evidence checker — makes sure every claim is backed by reasoning and evidence.
Maker or designer — builds the slides, poster or video.
Presenter — shares the finished outcome clearly with the audience.
Encourager — makes sure everyone is heard and draws in quieter members.

toolkit.title: Template: Roles and responsibilities
toolkit.intro: Copy this table and fill it in as a team. It makes objective 5.1 real: match each person's strength to a role, give them a clear task, and agree a deadline so the work is shared fairly.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for respectful disagreement
toolkit.intro: Use these to disagree about an idea without attacking the person. They keep a disagreement calm and point it towards agreement.
items: I see your point, and I wonder if ...
What if we combined both ideas by ...?
I understand why you think that. Could we also consider ...?
That could work. One thing I would add is ...
Help me understand your idea a bit more, then I will share mine.
Can we look for a middle way that uses the best of both?

toolkit.title: Giving and receiving feedback
toolkit.intro:
A simple, fair way to give feedback is two stars and a wish: two things that work well, then one thing that could be better. Always focus on the work, be kind but honest, and be specific.

When you receive feedback, use these four steps so it helps rather than stings:
items: Two things I really liked were ...
This part works well because ...
One thing that would make it even better is ...
Have you thought about trying ...?
This claim would be stronger with some evidence, such as ...
Listen without interrupting.
Thank the person for their help.
Do not rush to defend your work.
Choose one thing to act on, and change it.

toolkit.title: Template: Presentation review grid
toolkit.intro:
Copy this grid to evaluate another team's presentation fairly, or to check your own before you present. Judging work against clear criteria makes your feedback specific instead of just a feeling.

Finish with a highlight and one area for development, so your feedback gives both praise and a clear next step.

rows: Was there a suitable range of visuals (text, images, chart)?
Was the text large and clear enough for the audience?
Was there a clear structure (beginning, middle, end)?
Did the content answer the question and fit the aim?
Were the claims supported with reasoning and evidence?
Did the presenters make eye contact and speak clearly?
Was every member of the team involved?

toolkit.title: Template: Team review grid
toolkit.intro:
Copy this grid and complete it together when your outcome is finished. Answer honestly; an honest review is what makes the next project better.

Then finish two sentences together: 'We did best at ...' and 'Next time, we need to improve on ...'. Review each member's role fairly too, including your own.

rows: We finished our shared outcome on time.
Everyone contributed to the outcome.
We listened to and valued each other's ideas.
We supported our claims with reasoning and evidence.
We resolved disagreements and solved problems respectfully.
We used feedback to improve our work.

toolkit.title: How to run a fair team discussion
toolkit.intro: When your team needs to make a decision, a little structure keeps things fair and calm and stops the loudest voice from deciding everything.
items: Agree what you are deciding, in one sentence, so everyone is talking about the same thing.
Go around the team so each person shares one idea before anyone argues.
Ask your quietest member for their view, by name and kindly.
Look for a compromise that combines the best of the ideas.
Check that everyone can live with the decision before you move on.

toolkit.title: What to do when teamwork gets hard
toolkit.intro: Every team hits a rough patch; it does not mean the team has failed. Here are common problems and quick fixes:
items: One person is doing everything. Stop and share the work again using the roles table.
A member has gone quiet. Invite them in by name and ask what they think.
Two people keep clashing. Focus on the idea, not the person, and look for a compromise.
The team is stuck on a decision. Give each idea one minute, then choose the one that best fits the goal.
A claim has no evidence. Find evidence for it, or soften the claim to match what you can show.
Someone has not done their task. Ask kindly whether they need help, rather than blaming them.

toolkit.title: Signs your team is working well
toolkit.intro: Use this quick list to check the health of your team at any point in the project.
items: Everyone knows their role and what to do next.
Quieter members are speaking and being heard.
Disagreements are about ideas, not people.
Ideas are chosen because they fit the goal and have evidence, not because of who said them.
The team is making steady progress towards the shared outcome.

checklists.title: Checklist: Am I listening actively?
checklists.intro: Tick each one during a team discussion. Active listening is how you make everyone, especially quieter members, feel able to share.
items: Look at the speaker and do not interrupt.
Repeat their idea back: 'So you are saying ...'.
Ask a question to understand more, before making your own point.
Build on the idea with 'Yes, and ...' rather than 'No, but ...'.
Invite a quieter member to share, by name and kindly.

challenge.intro: Your team needs one shared topic that matters where you live, and a clear aim. Choosing them together is your first real act of collaboration. The best shared Challenge is one every member cares about a little, because you will all work on it for the rest of the unit. Choosing it fairly, where everyone is heard and the final choice belongs to the whole team, sets the tone for everything that follows.
checkpoints: I was surprised to discover that ...
I used to think that working as a team was ...
Now I think that working as a team is ...

activities.title: What makes an effective team?
activities.label: Activity 1: What makes an effective team?
activities.intro:
Before you form your team, warm up by thinking about what an effective team actually looks like. This helps you spot the habits you want in your group, and the habits in yourself you would like to grow. Imagine your team has been asked to organise a charity event for your school. Rank these ten characteristics from 1 (most important in a teammate) to 10 (least important):

There is no single correct order, but notice that some of these habits build a team up while others pull it down. Write your ranking, then write one sentence explaining your number one choice.
steps: Backs up claims with reasons and evidence

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your top three characteristics and your reasons.
Ask it: Which of these ten habits build a team up, and which pull it down?
Then tell the tutor which helpful habit you already show, and which one you would like to grow this unit.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Share your rankings with your team and compare them.
As a team, agree on the three characteristics you most want everyone to show.
Notice how your team reached agreement when your rankings were different.

activities.title: Map your strengths and agree roles (objective 5.1)
activities.label: Activity 3: Map your strengths and agree roles (objective 5.1)
activities.intro: A fair team divides work by strengths and by the time available. This is objective 5.1 in practice. First work out your own strengths, then agree the roles together. Remember that fair does not mean identical: it means the load is shared, everyone can use a strength, every job fits the time you have, and nobody, especially your quietest member, is left without a real job.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which team skills you are strong at: organising, listening, being creative, presenting, checking evidence, meeting deadlines, or encouraging others.
Ask it to help you list every job your shared outcome will need, and roughly how long each one will take.
Rehearse suggesting a fair split, and practise offering to take a job that fits your strength.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: As a team, fill in the roles-and-responsibilities table from your Skills Toolkit.
For each member, write their strength, their role, their main task, and a deadline.
Check together: is the work shared fairly, does it fit the time, and does everyone, including your quietest member, have a real job?
Write the finished roles into your teamwork journal, so no one forgets what they agreed to do.

activities.title: Contribute ideas with reasoning and evidence (objective 5.2)
activities.label: Activity 4: Contribute ideas with reasoning and evidence (objective 5.2)
activities.intro: A useful idea is one that is relevant to your shared goal and that you can back up. This is objective 5.2 in practice, with the Stage 8 habit of claim, reasoning and evidence. Practise generating ideas on your own, then choosing the best together. You are not trying to win; you are trying to give the team good, well-supported options.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Remind your AI tutor of your shared goal, then brainstorm at least five ideas for your outcome with it.
Take your strongest idea and turn it into a claim. Ask the tutor to help you add the reasoning (why you think it) and the evidence (how you know it).
Rehearse explaining that claim, reason and evidence in two or three clear sentences.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Each member offers their best idea as a claim, with a reason and any evidence. Nobody judges an idea by who said it.
As a team, decide which claims fit the goal and are well supported enough to belong in your outcome.
In your journal, note one claim you contributed and one from someone else that you helped strengthen with evidence.

Notice who found it easy to let an idea go, and who found it hard. Both feelings are completely normal. Letting go of your own idea for the good of the team is a real teamwork skill, and it gets easier every time you do it.

activities.title: Practise active listening and building on ideas
activities.label: Activity 5: Practise active listening and building on ideas
activities.intro: Active listening means showing you truly heard someone, then building on their idea with 'Yes, and ...'. This is how you draw in quieter members and how a group of individuals becomes a real team. It is a skill you can rehearse safely with your AI tutor before you use it with real people.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to pretend to be a teammate and share an idea about your topic.
Practise the moves: do not interrupt, repeat the idea back, ask a question, then build on it with the words Yes, and.
Ask the tutor for feedback: did you really listen, or were you just waiting to talk?

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Run a short team discussion where each person must repeat the previous idea before adding their own.
Make a point of inviting your quietest member to speak by name, and build on what they say.
Afterwards, ask each other: did everyone feel listened to?

If someone felt talked over, that is useful to know rather than something to feel bad about. Agree one small change together, such as letting each person finish before the next person speaks, and try it in your next session.

activities.title: Rehearse resolving a disagreement (objective 5.2)
activities.label: Activity 6: Rehearse resolving a disagreement (objective 5.2)
activities.intro: Disagreement is normal and can make ideas stronger. The skill, and part of objective 5.2, is to argue about the idea, kindly, and solve the problem together. This is the perfect thing to rehearse with your AI tutor, because it can play the person who disagrees with you without any of the real-life awkwardness. Practising the calm words now makes the real conversation much easier later.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe a disagreement your group might have, then ask your AI tutor to argue the opposite side to you.
Practise a polite sentence starter, such as: I see your point, and I wonder if we could combine both ideas.
Keep going until you and the tutor reach a compromise that uses the best of both ideas.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: When a real disagreement comes up, use the sentence starters instead of arguing to win.
Look for a compromise that combines both ideas rather than choosing one winner.
In your journal, record what the disagreement was and how your team solved it.

The goal of a disagreement is never to win, but to reach a decision the whole team can live with. A compromise that everyone accepts is far stronger than a victory that leaves one person feeling ignored.

activities.title: Gather local views fairly
activities.label: Activity 7: Gather local views fairly
activities.intro: A strong shared outcome uses real voices and real evidence from your community, not just facts from a book. To develop a local perspective, you need information from local people: your family, neighbours, shopkeepers, drivers and school staff. To stay fair and avoid bias, gather views from a range of people, not only those who already agree with you. Plan your questions with your tutor, then agree the best ones as a team and gather views together.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your topic and draft five interview questions about it.
Ask it to check that your questions are clear and fair, and not leading toward one answer.
Ask the tutor who you should interview so your evidence reflects the whole community, not just one view.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: As a team, share everyone's questions and agree on the best five to use.
Decide who will ask whom, and make sure your list includes a range of people so your evidence is not one-sided.

boxes.title: A real-world step
lines: With a trusted adult's help, ask your agreed questions to a few family members or neighbours.
Bring what you find back to your next teacher session so the team can use it as evidence in the shared outcome.

activities.title: Build your shared outcome and plan the presenting
activities.label: Activity 8: Build your shared outcome and plan the presenting
activities.intro: Now your team turns all its work into one shared outcome that fits its aim and audience. This is where objective 5.1 comes fully to life, because every member contributes the part that matches their role. Check your outcome has a clear beginning, middle and end, a mix of visuals, content that answers your question, and claims supported with evidence. Then plan how you will present it, so every member has a real speaking part.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what form your outcome will take and which part is your job.
Ask it to check your plan against the features of a strong outcome, and whether the form suits your aim.
Rehearse your own speaking part aloud, and ask the tutor for feedback on your clarity, pace and eye contact.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Bring each person's part together into one draft outcome.
Check as a team: does every claim have evidence, does the form fit the aim, and has everyone contributed?
Agree who will say which part when you present, so the presenting is shared, not left to one person.

Before you call the draft finished, check it against a simple list together: a clear structure; a mix of words and images; text large enough to read; content that answers your question with evidence; and a speaking part for everyone. Fix anything missing as a team.

activities.title: Evaluate another team's work and swap feedback
activities.label: Activity 9: Evaluate another team's work and swap feedback
activities.intro: Feedback makes a draft better, but only if it is specific, given kindly and received calmly. In Stage 8 you give feedback by evaluating work against clear criteria. Practise giving two stars and a wish, and receiving a wish without getting defensive. Rehearsing with your AI tutor helps, because it is easier to keep calm with a real person later once you have felt the words in practice.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe your draft outcome to your AI tutor and ask it to evaluate it against clear criteria, then give two stars and a wish.
Practise receiving the wish calmly: thank it, and name one specific change you will make.
Then rehearse giving kind, specific feedback on an imagined presentation, focusing on the work and not the person.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Swap your draft with another group and evaluate each other against the presentation criteria in your Skills Toolkit.
Give each other two stars and a wish, and check that your wish is specific and about the work.
Receive their feedback without arguing; thank them, and as a team make one clear improvement based on it.

activities.title: Review and improve your teamwork
activities.label: Activity 10: Review and improve your teamwork
activities.intro: When the outcome is finished, review honestly how your team worked, and how each member played their role. This is Collaboration meeting Reflection. A review that admits a weakness is far more useful than one that says everything was perfect, because it shows your team exactly what to do better next time.

boxes.title: Plan and Rehearse With Your AI Tutor
lines: Give your AI tutor an honest self-review of your own role: what did you contribute, and what could you do better?
Ask it to help you turn one honest thought into a fair, specific target, and to reflect kindly on a teammate's role too.

boxes.title: Do It With Your Group in Your Teacher Session
lines: Complete the team-review grid from your Skills Toolkit together.
Agree on one thing your team did best and one thing to improve next time.
Reflect on each member's role fairly. Being honest here is a strength, not a weakness.

Write your team's review into your teamwork journal. A team that reviews honestly, session after session, gets visibly better each time; a team that skips this step tends to keep repeating the same mistakes without noticing.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Try every question before you look at the answer key, and give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does 'collaboration' mean?
practice.answer: Collaboration means working with others towards a shared goal, sharing the work fairly, so together you make something better than one person could alone. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: True or false: an effective team is made of people who are all good at exactly the same things.
practice.answer: False. An effective team is made of different people whose strengths fit together.

practice.prompt: Cambridge objective 5.1 is about dividing roles and tasks how? (a) equally by size (b) fairly, by strengths and time available (c) by who talks loudest.
practice.answer: (b) fairly, by strengths and time available.

practice.prompt: A claim is stronger when it is supported by two things. Name them.
practice.answer: Reasoning (why I think it) and evidence (how I know it).

practice.prompt: A useful idea is one that is ______ to the shared goal.
practice.answer: Relevant.

practice.prompt: Which starter helps you build on someone's idea: 'No, but ...' or 'Yes, and ...'?
practice.answer: 'Yes, and ...'.

practice.prompt: When you disagree in a team, should you argue against the person or against the idea?
practice.answer: The idea, never the person.

practice.prompt: Two different ideas combined into a better third idea is called a ______.
practice.answer: A compromise.

practice.prompt: What is the aim of a shared outcome? Answer the question it is meant to answer.
practice.answer: The aim is the purpose of the outcome; it answers 'What are we hoping to achieve?'.

practice.prompt: In the feedback method 'two stars and a wish', what is the wish?
practice.answer: The one thing that could be better (the area for improvement).

practice.prompt: True or false: when someone gives you feedback, you should defend your work straight away.
practice.answer: False. You should listen, thank them, and not defend your work straight away.

practice.prompt: Name one thing you should check when you evaluate another team's presentation.
practice.answer: Any one of: were the visuals suitable; was the structure clear; were claims supported with evidence; did the presenters make eye contact and speak clearly; was every member involved.

practice.prompt: What is bias, and why should a fair team try to avoid it?
practice.answer: Bias is judging from only one point of view and refusing to consider others. A fair team avoids it so its evidence and conclusions reflect the whole community, not just one side.

practice.prompt: In our model, who is your planning and rehearsal partner, and where does the real teamwork happen?
practice.answer: My AI tutor is my planning and rehearsal partner; the real teamwork happens with my group in my teacher sessions (and with family and community).

practice.prompt: Give one reason why every member of a team should have a speaking part when the team presents.
practice.answer: Any sensible reason, such as: it is fairer; it shows the work is genuinely shared; it keeps every member involved; it is stronger than one person doing everything.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each collaboration word (1 to 8) to the correct meaning (A to H). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Collaboration
options: A. Something a team produces together, such as a presentation, poster or video.
B. Honest, kind, specific advice about a piece of work, meant to help improve it.
C. Working with others towards a shared goal to make something better than one person could alone.
D. Judging from only one point of view and refusing to consider others.
E. Showing a speaker you truly heard them, then building on their idea.
F. An agreement that combines the best of two different ideas.
G. A statement that something is true, which needs support to be believed.
H. The facts, observations or interviews that show a claim is true.
practice.answer: C — Working with others towards a shared goal to make something better than one person could alone.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Shared outcome
practice.answer: A — Something a team produces together, such as a presentation, poster or video.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Compromise
practice.answer: F — An agreement that combines the best of two different ideas.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Active listening
practice.answer: E — Showing a speaker you truly heard them, then building on their idea.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Feedback
practice.answer: B — Honest, kind, specific advice about a piece of work, meant to help improve it.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Claim
practice.answer: G — A statement that something is true, which needs support to be believed.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Evidence
practice.answer: H — The facts, observations or interviews that show a claim is true.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Bias
practice.answer: D — Judging from only one point of view and refusing to consider others.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Nadir keeps offering ideas that do not fit the goal, and the team is running out of time. What could the team say to keep him contributing usefully?
practice.answer: Thank Nadir for his energy, then gently ask the team to check each idea against the goal and the time left, so his ideas stay useful.

practice.prompt: Dina has a good idea but has not spoken all session. What is one thing Grace could do to bring her in?
practice.answer: Grace could look at Dina, invite her by name to share, repeat her idea back, and build on it so she feels heard.

practice.prompt: Talia wants to aim the presentation at drivers and Malik wants to aim it at the school. Suggest a compromise that uses both ideas.
practice.answer: Aim at both: speak to drivers and the school, and end with two clear requests, one for each. Both ideas are used.

practice.prompt: A slide claims 'this crossing is the most dangerous in the city' but shows no evidence. What should the team do before using it?
practice.answer: Do not use the claim until it has evidence. Add the traffic count or an interview, or soften the claim to match what the evidence actually shows.

practice.prompt: Another group tells your team one slide has too much text. You feel like arguing. What should you do instead?
practice.answer: Do not argue. Thank the other group, talk it over as a team, and choose one change to make, such as cutting some text.

practice.prompt: Your team finished on time but one person did nearly all the presenting. What honest target should the team set for next time?
practice.answer: A fair target such as: next time we will share the presenting so every member has a speaking part.

reflection.prompt: Planning and rehearsing on my own with my AI tutor before the real teamwork ...
Doing the real collaboration with my group in teacher sessions ...
Working with my family or community ...
Writing what happened in my teamwork journal as I went ...

vocabulary.meaning: Working with others towards a shared goal so you make something better than one person could alone.
A group of people working together towards a shared outcome.
Something a team produces together, such as a presentation, poster or video.
The purpose of a shared outcome; what the team hopes to achieve.
The particular job a person takes on within a team.
A task you have agreed to do for the team.
Something a team member is good at, such as organising or listening.
Something you add to the team, such as an idea, a task done, or encouragement.
Actually useful for reaching your shared goal.
A statement that something is true, which needs support to be believed.
The thinking that explains why you believe a claim; it answers 'Why do I think this?'.
The facts, observations or interviews that show a claim is true; it answers 'How do I know this?'.
Judging from only one point of view and refusing to consider others.
The point of view someone has, shaped by who they are and where they live.
Showing a speaker you truly heard them, then building on their idea.
Adding to someone's idea to make it stronger, often with the words 'Yes, and ...'.
A disagreement between team members.
An agreement that combines the best of two different ideas.
Working helpfully alongside others.
Honest, kind, specific advice about a piece of work, meant to help improve it.
A feedback method: two things done well, and one thing to improve.
The clear points you judge a piece of work against.
Looking back honestly at how well a team worked together.
Taking an active part in the team's work.
To help someone feel able to take part and share their ideas.
The time by which a task must be finished.
Quickly listing many ideas without judging them yet.
An early version of your outcome that you will improve.
The people your shared outcome is made for.
A small, clear thing you aim to improve next time.
Honestly judging your own work and progress.

mistakes: Dividing work by who talks loudest instead of by strengths and time.
Leaving your quietest member with no real role.
Judging an idea by who said it rather than whether it fits the goal.
Putting claims in your outcome with no reasoning or evidence behind them.
Arguing to win instead of looking for a compromise.
Giving feedback that attacks the person instead of the work.
Letting one person do all the presenting.
Ending a project without an honest review of how the team worked.

selfAssessment.statement: I understand what the word 'collaboration' means.
I can name my own strengths as a team member.
I can help my team divide roles and tasks fairly, by strength and time (5.1).
I can contribute useful ideas backed by reasoning and evidence (5.2).
I can listen actively and encourage a quieter member to take part.
I can resolve a disagreement respectfully and help solve a problem (5.2).
I can help build a shared outcome that fits its aim and audience.
I can give feedback that is specific, kind and about the work.
I can receive feedback without getting defensive.
I can review honestly how well my team, and I, worked.
